# Scalability & Extensibility

Our solution is modular in structure and selectively parametrised in behaviour. Modularity allows responsibilities to change independently, whereas parametrisation changes a component's behaviour without
changing its code. The backend separates context loading, deterministic engines, targeted LLM steps, Advisor tools, prompts, session persistence, and observability. For example, the modal-shift
engine accepts the feasibility judge as an optional callable and can use the LLM implementation, a test double, or its deterministic fallback. One scoring
primitive is reused by the initial analysis, modal-shift ranking, and chat-driven re-optimisation, so corrections propagate across all three paths. Behaviour is parametrised through the
onboarding weights for cost, CO~2~, and flexibility. The scoring engine maps flexibility to estimated travel time, the only quantified proxy currently available. Further parameters
include the forecast horizon, output language, and the constraints passed from what-if requests into the re-optimisation engine. Operational settings such as the model endpoint,
pool and worker sizes, LLM concurrency, timeouts, and retries are environment variables. The solution is therefore adaptable but not fully configuration-driven. Adding an Advisor
capability still requires a deterministic tool, its registration, a prompt instruction, and tests. A provider that fits an existing category and pricing model can
usually be added through a catalogue row and an Open Knowledge Format Markdown document. New categories, scoring dimensions, or pricing models still require coordinated
code changes across backend and frontend components.

Several measures support moderate growth. Per-user queries are indexed, PostgreSQL connections are pooled, and the mostly static pricing catalogue is cached. A stored session
snapshot prevents the dashboard from repeating analysis and model calls unnecessarily. On a fresh run, the deterministic result is returned before forecast reasoning and
modal-shift feasibility run concurrently in the background. A process-wide concurrency limit queues excess LLM calls instead of overwhelming the shared university endpoint. This protects
the pilot under bursts but does not add throughput. At production scale, `load_context` should filter and pre-aggregate long trip histories in SQL or materialised
views instead of processing every leg in Python. The growing tariff corpus would need indexed metadata or full-text search, document chunking, and selective context.
Long conversations would also require retention rules or summaries. Because background jobs, caches, and the LLM semaphore currently live inside one backend process, horizontal
scaling would require an external job queue, coordinated rate limits, and stateless API instances behind a load balancer. The free university-hosted LLM endpoint is
suitable for the prototype but lacks production capacity and service guarantees. A larger deployment would need a production quota, a commercial OpenAI-compatible provider, or
a self-hosted model. Centralised model access and configurable connection settings limit the necessary code changes, although any replacement must be re-evaluated for structured output,
tool selection, latency, privacy, and cost.

The same component boundaries also simplify maintenance. `agent/llm.py` centralises model access and retries, `session.py` owns snapshots, transcripts, and revisions, and deterministic engines can be
tested without a database or model endpoint. The simulate--confirm--apply boundary isolates the Advisor tool layer's only state-changing capability. Typed models would make schema changes
safer than the current nested dictionaries. Removing remaining compatibility structures such as the repurposed `optimizer_scenarios` column and replacing first-run SQL initialisation with managed migrations
would further improve maintainability.
